slides: Open by making crystallography a story about repetition plus constraints. A wallpaper pattern begins with translations, but the geometry becomes interesting when cells, motifs, half-turns, glides, rotations, and ordinary-line phenomena are checked against the lattice rather than merely seen as ornament.

Use the route slide to keep the chapter from becoming a list of wallpaper examples. The lecture builds from a lattice basis to a Dirichlet cell, then attaches motifs, compares brick symmetries, proves why only certain rotation orders survive, and ends with tessellation and collinearity checks.

The lattice slide should establish the basic unit. Every lattice point is an integer combination of two independent translations, and the fundamental parallelogram area equals the determinant. The Dirichlet cell is the nearest-neighbor version of a fundamental region, with six neighbors in this oblique example.

The motif slide separates lattice symmetry from decorative content. The left pattern uses translations only, while the right pattern adds a glide reflection. The important relation is that applying the glide twice gives a full translation, so the motif carries extra symmetry information.

Brick patterns provide a familiar diagnostic surface. A single two-to-one rectangle may look simple, but different offsets and orientations preserve different global symmetries. The six schematics mark mirrors, glides, half-turns, and quarter-turns so students inspect which local brick symmetries survive globally.

The crystallographic restriction is the conceptual center of the chapter. A lattice-preserving rotation must act by an integer matrix, so its trace equals two cosine of the rotation angle and must be an integer. That leaves exactly the orders two, three, four, and six.

The tessellation slide connects crystallography to regular tilings. The vertex angle equation gives the finite list of Euclidean regular tessellations, and the adjacency graph makes the dual operation concrete: faces become graph vertices and shared edges become graph edges.

The ordinary-line slide changes from infinite repetition to finite point sets. The determinant test identifies collinearity, while the ordinary-line count shows that a generic finite noncollinear set cannot hide all two-point lines. The minimum-distance scaffold previews the geometric proof idea.

The Dirichlet angle lab gives students a controlled parameter experiment. With equal-length generators, the Voronoi cell stays area-correct as the angle changes, but its side count changes from hexagonal behavior to a square at ninety degrees when opposite sides collapse.

Close by tying the parts together. Two-dimensional crystallography is not only a catalog of patterns; it is a set of constraints on translations, cells, motifs, rotations, and finite point configurations. The checks make those constraints visible as determinant areas, traces, adjacency graphs, and ordinary lines.
